title: arXiv AI weekly | 2–9 October 2026 | 8 notable papers
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart; this is an inferred shortlist, not a comprehensive ranking. Citation evidence is limited for papers this recent.

sections.title: Training Advisors for LLM Agents from Task Outcomes
sections.abstract: Caddie trains a language-model critic with reinforcement learning from final task success; the authors report transfer across agents and interactive benchmarks without step-level labels or reference critiques.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce outcome-trained natural-language advice for agents during execution, while keeping the base agent frozen.
sections.unique_caveat: Reported transfer starts from one Qwen3-4B critic-training setup; performance beyond tested agents, benchmarks, and invocation protocols remains unestablished.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Three core AI-category cross-lists, independent indexing, and reported transfer to additional base models and out-of-domain tasks.

sections.title: CurveTQ: Rotation-Free Trellis Quantization of LLM Weights via Curvature-Weighted Search
sections.abstract: CurveTQ uses Hessian-curvature weights in trellis search to quantize model weights without rotations; the authors report improved accuracy over two-bit baselines on tested models and faster decoding.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors incorporate diagonal Hessian information into Viterbi branch costs and build a native-basis codec that avoids decoding-time rotations.
sections.unique_caveat: Evidence covers a limited set of model families and bit-widths; the reported accuracy and speed advantages need broader replication.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Cross-listed in machine learning and AI; directly compares two-bit accuracy across three 4–8B instruction models and one 35B MoE and reports decoding speed.

sections.title: Noise Your Prompt: Noising Conditioning Tokens in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
sections.abstract: The paper adds noise to conditioning tokens during training of continuous diffusion language models; the author reports gains on Sudoku, N-Queens, and Gigaword summarization, but not open-ended dialogue.
sections.claimed_contribution: The author reports improved harder-Sudoku solve rates and N-Queens solution coverage without default inference-cost increases.
sections.unique_caveat: The author explicitly reports no gains for open-ended dialogue; positive results are task-dependent and include modest-data summarization settings.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: TMLR journal reference and a v2 revision during the selected window; evaluation spans reasoning and language-generation tasks.

sections.title: Agent Behavior as Code: Efficient and Robust LLM Agents with Programmatic Specifications
sections.abstract: ABCAgent turns reusable agent behavior into editable programs; the authors report improved robustness and reduced cost or latency on selected benchmarks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors specify agent behavior with a symbolic runtime program that a foundation-model agent can edit.
sections.unique_caveat: Strong results are benchmark- and task-family-specific; the evaluation does not establish generalization to arbitrary open-ended tasks.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Cross-listed in AI, language, and multiagent systems; evaluated on six benchmarks, including two constructed for task-variant generalization.

sections.title: Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent LLM Inference: What It Costs, What It Buys, and When You Can Tell
sections.abstract: In a three-tier agent setup, the authors measure lower peak KV-cache use from inference decomposition but no detectable accuracy change from persistent reasoning-trace memory on their single-question benchmarks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors set out conditions and detection procedures for meaningful agent-memory ablations, arguing their benchmark setup gives stored traces nothing useful to retrieve.
sections.unique_caveat: The null result is limited to one three-tier architecture and single-question datasets; it does not establish that memory is useless for tasks requiring accumulated evidence.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Four-category cross-listing, acceptance as a NeurIPS 2026 Machine Learning for Systems Workshop poster, independent indexing, and controlled memory/cache measurements.

sections.title: How RL Reshapes LLM Reasoning: Transferability, Coverage, and Scaling Laws
sections.abstract: Across Qwen and Gemma models, the authors analyze how reinforcement learning changes reasoning strategies, cross-domain transfer, and solution coverage, and develop a strategy-selection model with scaling-law analyses.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors argue that RL can reweight existing reasoning strategies, changing task performance and coverage without necessarily expanding strategy support.
sections.unique_caveat: The empirical scope is Qwen and Gemma families; theoretical conclusions depend on the two-stage strategy-selection abstraction.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Three core AI/ML category cross-lists; combines experiments across two model families with a formal account of transfer and coverage changes.

sections.title: PsyCIDRA: A Dual-Agent Framework for Psychiatric Interviewing and Diagnostic Reasoning
sections.abstract: PsyCIDRA separates interactive psychiatric interviewing from diagnostic reasoning; the authors report improved agreement over direct prompting on simulated cases and in a blinded human-participant study.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine tool-supported interviewing, working notes, expert-written skills, and ICD-11 retrieval with a separate evidence-reporting diagnostic agent.
sections.unique_caveat: Patient profiles are simulated and the human-participant study does not establish improved real-world clinical outcomes or readiness for deployment.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: A domain-specific agent study with explicit evaluation of interview, diagnosis, and safety; reports separate simulated and participant sample sizes.

sections.title: Shared and structured inputs undermine collective random choice by reasoning AI agents
sections.abstract: Behavioral tests across reasoning models find that identifier patterns can make supposedly random agent choices biased or correlated; explicit randomization instructions reduce but do not eliminate the effect.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors show that selection rates alone can miss input-dependent bias, correlation, and predictability in model-based random selection.
sections.unique_caveat: Results are behavioral tests on a small set of models and specified identifiers; prevalence in deployed allocation or audit systems is not established.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: A cross-disciplinary test of a concrete agent-oversight failure mode; Semantic Scholar listed 0 citations at the snapshot.
